matching.reasoningTemplate: Headache and fluctuating consciousness after a fall, especially elderly/anticoagulated, suggests a subdural haematoma.

clinicalPearls: Direct cranial trauma may be minor and is not always required for an acute subdural bleed, particularly in the elderly and those on anticoagulants; acceleration forces alone (e.g. whiplash) can suffice (p.3572).
Up to one-third of patients with acute subdural haematoma have a lucid interval of minutes to hours before coma supervenes, but most are drowsy or comatose from the moment of injury (p.3572).
A unilateral headache with a slightly enlarged pupil on the side of the haematoma is frequently, though not invariably, present (p.3572).
Small subdural haematomas may be asymptomatic and usually do not require evacuation unless they enlarge (p.3572).
In chronic subdural haematoma, drowsiness, inattentiveness and incoherent thinking are generally more prominent than focal signs such as hemiparesis (p.3573).
Chronic subdural haematoma headache typically fluctuates in severity, sometimes with changes in head position (p.3573).
A history of trauma may be absent in chronic subdural haematoma; the injury may have been trivial and forgotten, especially in the elderly and those with clotting disorders (p.3572).
Recurrent falls in older adults place them at risk for subdural haematoma; brain imaging is warranted when neurologic signs are present (pp.222-223, 3927, 3929).
Trauma should be considered in any patient with an unexplained acute neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, stupor, confusion), particularly after a fall (p.3498).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bleeding occurs beneath the dura (subdural space). The bleeding producing larger subdural haematomas is primarily venous in origin, classically from torn bridging veins, although arterial bleeding sites are occasionally found at operation and a few large haematomas are purely arterial. Chronic subdural haematomas develop days to weeks after (often trivial) injury, favoured by age-related cerebral atrophy that stretches bridging veins; they organise into a vascular fibrous capsule, and weeks-old collections often contain a mixture of blood and serous fluid. Anticoagulant-related intracranial haemorrhages are often subdural and may continue to evolve over 24-48 h if coagulopathy is insufficiently reversed (pp.3572-3573, 3498).
additionalDifferentials: Epidural haematoma (lenticular/lens-shaped on CT, usually arterial from a torn middle meningeal artery, classic lucid interval, more rapid evolution)
Cerebral contusion / convexity contusion (can produce focal deficits such as aphasia or mild hemiparesis)
Carotid or vertebral artery dissection (can mimic focal deficits seen with subdural)
Posttraumatic headache syndrome (chronic subdural may mimic this) (p.160)
nonInfectiousMimics: Transient ischemic attack (rarely chronic subdural causes brief episodes of hemiparesis or aphasia indistinguishable from TIA) (p.3573)
Dementia / Alzheimer or other neurodegenerative disease (chronic subdural is a treatable cause of dementia, often on a background of cortical atrophy) (pp.238, 3527)
Stroke (subdural is considered when excluding stroke in older fallers) (p.3929)
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus and other reversible dementia causes (listed alongside subdural among treatable dementias) (p.238)
additionalInvestigations: MRI reliably identifies both subacute and chronic subdural haematomas and is useful when CT is equivocal (p.3573)
Contrast-enhanced imaging demonstrates enhancement of the vascular fibrous capsule surrounding a chronic collection (p.3573)
Serial imaging for clinical observation of small chronic collections without mass effect (p.3573)
redFlags: Stupor or coma, hemiparesis, and unilateral pupillary enlargement indicate a larger acute haematoma (p.3572)
Acutely deteriorating patient requiring emergency craniotomy (p.3572)
Repetitive vomiting, nystagmus, drowsiness and unsteadiness may signal a posterior fossa subdural haematoma (p.3619)
Large bleed after only minor trauma should raise concern for coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy (p.3573)
harrison.prognosis: In contrast to epidural haematomas, acute subdural haematomas requiring surgery carry significant morbidity and mortality, partly reflecting frequently associated underlying cortical brain damage. Chronic subdural collections evacuated through burr holes are usually treated successfully when a postoperative cranial drain is used; encapsulating fibrous membranes may require craniotomy to prevent recurrent fluid accumulation (pp.3572-3573).
pitfalls: Subacute pitfall: between roughly 2 and 6 weeks after the initial bleed the clot becomes isodense relative to adjacent brain on non-contrast CT and may be inapparent/missed (p.3573).

Acute subdural produces more horizontal displacement (mass effect) than expected from its thickness because of its large rostral-caudal extent, so mass effect can be underestimated from clot thickness alone (p.3572).
Absence of a trauma history does not exclude chronic subdural haematoma in the elderly or anticoagulated (p.3572).
Skull fractures are markers of injury site/severity, not the haematoma itself, and may be absent (p.3572).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames subdural haematoma by acuity and imaging appearance rather than a numeric grade: ACUTE — non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense crescentic clot with an irregular brain interface (Fig. 454-2); SUBACUTE (~2-6 weeks) — clot becomes isodense and easily overlooked, often with mixed blood and serous fluid; CHRONIC — hypodense crescentic collection over one or both convexities, most often frontotemporal (Fig. 454-3) (pp.3572-3573).
